title: failed prototype, wasted a few hours
author: Square-Yam-3772
selftext:
I basically mixed a few ways to generate sprite and animations and the resolution ended up looking all over the place. I also tried to "deep fried" the spritesheet as an attempt to hide the imperfections. It totally didn't work out

the gameplay decision of "light up the screen once a while with an action" also seem kind of dumb once I see it in action. 

but even a prototype like this is quite taxing on gen credits: 7 animations for the hero and 4 animations for the boss. 

aseprite came in clutch though. 

Images 2.0 probably need another upgrade before I can lean on it for more animations. It is too hit-or-miss right now

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: actually, it looks slightly more serviceable on my phone. I guess I just need to fix the boss's resolution to closer to the background/player. Maybe it is salvageable, no idea...

comments.body: Yeah this looks pretty bad, like when devs first started using digitized human sprites in the 1980s lol. Are you saying you failed prototyping game mechanics or just the sprite generation stuff? Cause it would be crazy to spend resources to make sprites while prototyping gameplay.

replies.body: it is both. I am experimenting with sprite/animation generation mostly. prototyping gameplay via vibe coding is pretty easy.

comments.author: Cool-Chemical-5629
comments.body: This doesn't look terrible. Let's be honest, what you see as merely a failed prototype, someone else would see as a product ready for selling, at least in early access. If you like working on something because it's going well so far and you can see how it's shaping for better over time, just keep going until you're satisfied. I'm not making too complex games, but even simple games take a lot of time. What looks simple on surface is usually very complex behind the scenes in the code.
